title: The first week
hook: sin and mercy, ending in a conversation at the foot of the cross
carry: what have I done for christ

segments.voice: Yesterday, indifference: not a shrug, but balance, holding created things open until the way is clear. Your line was hold it loosely. Which preference did you manage to loosen, even a little? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-three.

The first week of the Exercises is not gentle. Ignatius asks the person praying to look at sin, the world's and then their own, plainly, without excuses. Old arguments. Things said that can't be unsaid. It would be easy to stop there, stuck in a pile of regret. He doesn't let it end there. At the close of the hour he moves the person somewhere else: to the foot of the cross, face to face, and talking. Not reciting. Talking. Today's word is the name he gives that talk.
screen: `LOOK AT SIN, PLAINLY.` → `DON'T STOP THERE.` → `GO TO THE FOOT OF THE CROSS.`

segments.voice: A colloquy is a conversation. Ignatius says to make it the way one friend speaks to another, or the way a servant speaks to a master: asking for something, admitting something, saying what's on your mind and asking for advice. In the first week he sets the scene. Imagine Christ our Lord in front of you, hanging on the cross. Ask how it is that the Creator became human, and went from eternal life to death, for my sins. Then turn to yourself with three questions. What have I done for Christ? What am I doing for Christ? What ought I to do for Christ? Watch the direction change. The week began with sin, and sin can turn a person inward, into shame. The colloquy turns them outward, toward a face. The questions are not a scorecard. They come after the person has spent time looking at someone who loved first. Saint Paul has a line in Galatians that fits the scene, in the Douay-Rheims: the Son of God, "who loved me, and delivered himself for me." Me, singular. Ignatius also asks the one praying to wonder at something easy to miss: that they've been allowed to go on living, that the earth has held them up, that mercy kept the door open. So the first week runs sin, then mercy, then conversation. And the Exercises don't script the colloquy. Ignatius closes it with an Our Father, a prayer the Church already has, but the talk before it belongs to the one praying. Outside a retreat, the difference still holds. Guilt alone tends to spin in place. A conversation goes somewhere.
screen: `COLLOQUY: A CONVERSATION.` · `AS ONE FRIEND SPEAKS TO ANOTHER.` · `THREE QUESTIONS AT THE CROSS.` · `SIN, THEN MERCY, THEN TALK.` · then, large: `WHO LOVED ME, AND DELIVERED HIMSELF FOR ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a conversation at the cross. Settle, and breathe. If there's a crucifix nearby, look at it; if not, let the image come to mind. If you pray, speak to Christ on the cross in your own words, the way you'd talk to a friend at a hospital bedside. Say what's true. Ask for what you need. Then let the first question sit there: what have I done for Christ? If you don't pray, you can stay with the image of someone who gave something up for you, and ask what you've done in return. No need to fill the silence. The bell holds the time.

Colloquy. A conversation, as one friend speaks to another, here at the foot of the cross. This week ran from Dominic's last promise to his brothers into the first week of Ignatius's Exercises. Today's word.
Your line: what have I done for Christ. Tonight, before sleep, ask it once, then ask the other two: what am I doing, and what ought I to do. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: In the first week of an Ignatian retreat, people pray over sin and God's mercy, and end each prayer time with a colloquy, an unscripted conversation with Christ, often closed with the Our Father.

options: keep listing them until you've found every one.
turn to Christ on the cross and talk, as to a friend.
put it away and think about something cheerful.
fork.reveal: Ignatius closes the meditation with a colloquy: a face, three questions, and an Our Father. sin is looked at, then mercy, then talk.

original.note: Spanish, the word Ignatius uses in the Exercises: a conversation, a talk between two.

trapdoor: what you thought: a colloquy is a formal meeting of experts.
what it means: in the Exercises, it's an honest talk with Christ, the way one friend speaks to another.
what a scholar hears: Ignatius closes the first week's meditation on sin at the cross, with three questions and an Our Father, and leaves the words in between to the one praying.
